introduction: Some twenty thousand people died for the faith of the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh in its first decades, and these passages speak of them: what was done to them and how they met it, the insistence that they were killed and did not kill, the meaning of sacrifice, care for the families left behind, prayers for the dead, and the claim that such blood makes a cause grow. They also say that service through a long life can be worth more than a death. A hundred voices stand beside them: the suffering servant of Isaiah, Stephen and Paul, Polycarp, Ignatius and Tertullian, the Qur’an on those slain in God's way, Socrates before his judges, Pericles and Lincoln over the dead; and Milton, Yeats, Owen, Nietzsche and Mill, who ask what such deaths prove and what they cost.
questions: "Praise be to God that ye were slain in His path but slew not." How does that sentence separate these deaths from other kinds of dying for a cause, such as the kind Wilfred Owen wrote about?
One talk says that a person who longs for martyrdom should arise to serve. Ignatius of Antioch begged not to be rescued. What is the place of the wish to die in these readings?
Nietzsche said that blood is the worst witness to truth, and Mill that persecution often succeeds. What do the martyrs show, and what do they not?
Milton cried for vengeance on the killers of the faithful. What do these passages ask for in its place?
Several letters comfort parents and children of the dead. Compare them with David's cry for Absalom and Lincoln's letter to a mother. What can be said to the bereaved?
Jesus said that those who build the prophets' tombs are the children of those who killed them. What is the right way to remember martyrs?

outside.why: Jesus says that no one takes his life from him: he lays it down of himself.
Paul told his weeping friends that he was ready not only to be bound but to die at Jerusalem.
The Preacher says that to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose.
Paul asks believers to present their bodies a living sacrifice, which he calls their reasonable service.

Ignatius of Antioch begged the church at Rome not to save him from the beasts, so that he might be ground like wheat. This talk tells the one who longs for martyrdom to arise and serve. When should the wish to die for a cause be turned into something else?
In the Qur’an Abel says to his brother: even if thou stretch out thy hand to kill me, I shall not stretch out mine to kill thee.
Jesus tells Peter to put up his sword, for all who take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Three young men told a king that they would not bow to his image, whether or not God delivered them from the furnace.
Jesus prayed from the cross: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
Stephen, the first Christian martyr, died asking that his death not be laid to his killers' charge.
Paul asks believers to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep.
Jesus says: resist not evil; whoever strikes thee on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.
Peter says of Christ that when he was reviled he did not revile in return, and when he suffered he did not threaten.
Jesus warned his disciples that a time would come when whoever killed them would think he was doing God service.
Habakkuk was told to write the vision and make it plain, for it is for an appointed time.
The letter to the Hebrews remembers those who were stoned, sawn asunder and slain with the sword, of whom the world was not worthy.
A psalm says: for thy sake we are killed all the day long.
The Revelation of John says of the martyrs that they loved not their lives unto the death.
Jesus says that there is no greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends.
Paul says that God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the mighty.
Tertullian told the persecutors of his day that the blood of Christians is seed.
Isaiah's servant is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and opens not his mouth.
The Qur’an says: think not of those slain in the way of God as dead; they are living, and provided for.
Genesis says that the voice of Abel's blood cried from the ground.
The Song of Songs says that love is strong as death, and that floods cannot drown it.
Yeats, writing of men executed for their cause, feared that too long a sacrifice can make a stone of the heart. What keeps a love that welcomes death from hardening?
Paul says near his end: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.
Jesus counts among his own those who came to him in prison.
John sees a multitude in white robes who have come out of great tribulation.
Jesus told his disciples that they would be brought before governors and kings, and that the Spirit would speak in them.
The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer.
The Qur’an recalls the companions of earlier prophets, who did not weaken for what befell them in the way of God.
The aged Polycarp, urged to save himself, said that he had served his Lord eighty-six years and received no wrong.
The Revelation of John says: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Peter tells his readers not to think the fiery trial strange, but to rejoice as sharers in Christ's sufferings.
Jesus calls blessed those who are persecuted and reviled for his sake.
Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted.
Milton, hearing of a massacre of believers in the Alps, cried: avenge, O Lord, thy slaughtered saints. What do these letters do with the wish for vengeance?
Tertullian reports the cry raised in his day at every calamity: the Christians to the lion!
Jesus laments over a city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it.
Jesus says of those who build the tombs of the prophets that they are the children of those who killed them. What is the use of mourning the martyrs of an earlier age?
Jesus tells his disciples that in the world they shall have tribulation, and to be of good cheer.
Jesus says that whoever would follow him must take up his cross.
The Gita says that the spirit was never born and shall never cease to be; it is not slain when the body is slain.
Paul writes: I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
Paul calls God the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort.
The Qur’an says of believers burned in a ditch that their killers had nothing against them save that they believed in God.
The letter to the Hebrews speaks of those who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
John records that at the grave of a friend, with the mourners around him, Jesus wept.
Lamentations asks: is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow.
Pericles said over the Athenian dead that heroes have the whole earth for their tomb.
Lincoln said at Gettysburg that the living cannot hallow such ground; those who struggled there have consecrated it.
Jesus says that a grain of wheat bears much fruit only if it dies.
Gibbon tells how a persecuted religion at last raised its banner over the ruins of the empire that had tried to destroy it.
A psalm says: precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
The first letter of John asks for love in deed and in truth toward a brother in need.
Thoreau wrote that under a government which imprisons unjustly, the true place for a just man is a prison.
Lovelace wrote from prison that stone walls do not make one, nor iron bars a cage.
Paul is persuaded that neither death nor life can separate us from the love of God.
Lincoln wrote to a mother who had lost her sons of the solemn pride that must be hers.
Simeon told the mother of Jesus that a sword would pierce through her own soul also.
Job says, when his children are dead: the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.
Paul says: to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
Wilfred Owen, who saw men die in the trenches, called the saying that it is sweet to die for one's country the old lie. How is the praise of martyrdom here different from the praise he condemned?
Daniel says that the wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and as the stars for ever.
Genesis tells of Abraham, ready to offer his son, his only son.
David cried for his dead son: would God I had died for thee. What is asked of a parent in the passage here, and what is not denied?
Paul says that those who condemned Jesus fulfilled the prophets that were read to them every sabbath.
Proverbs says that the memory of the just is blessed, and the name of the wicked shall rot.
Paul says that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
Job says: though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
Isaiah says of God that in all their affliction he was afflicted.
The letter to the Hebrews speaks of a great cloud of witnesses who surround those still running the race.
Jesus asks two disciples whether they can drink of the cup that he drinks of.
Paul asks believers to bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Paul asks the bereaved not to sorrow as those who have no hope.
A psalm calls God a father of the fatherless and a judge of the widows.
Paul lists the perils he lived among while teaching: beatings, stonings, journeys, dangers in every place.
A psalm sings of the soul escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers.
Lamentations weeps over a city left solitary, with none to comfort her.
Jesus prayed, the night before he died, that all who believed might be one.
Nietzsche wrote that blood is the very worst witness to truth. What does the willingness of twenty thousand to die show, and what does it not?
Zechariah heard that it is not by might, nor by power, but by the Spirit.
Paul says: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
Paul says that he has suffered the loss of all things and counts them as nothing.
A psalm says that God keeps his servant's tears in a bottle and writes them in his book.
The first Christians met daily, breaking bread with gladness and singleness of heart.
John sees the souls of the slain under the altar, crying: how long, O Lord?
The letter of James says to count it all joy when trials come.
The first letter of John says: love not the world, neither the things that are in the world.
Jesus says that whoever loses his life for his sake shall save it.
Dickens gives Sydney Carton, dying in another man's place, the words: it is a far, far better thing that I do than I have ever done. What makes a death given for another count as a gift?
Socrates told his judges that no evil can happen to a good man, in life or after death.
In the parable those who came at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who bore the heat of the day.
Gamaliel warned a council that what is of God cannot be overthrown by killing its teachers.
Mill called it a pleasant falsehood that truth always triumphs over persecution: history is full of truths put down. What do these passages rest their confidence on?
Job says that there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again.
Socrates, sentenced, said that there is great reason to hope that death is a good.
Jesus tells his followers that a candle is not lit to be hidden, but to give light to all.
Isaiah foretells that the wilderness shall be glad and the desert shall blossom as the rose.

revelation-loved-not-their-lives.text: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death

acts-ready-to-die-at-jerusalem.text: Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus

john-i-lay-down-my-life.text: Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father

genesis-thine-only-son.text: And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son. And the angel of the Lord called unto him out of heaven, and said, Abraham, Abraham: and he said, Here am I. And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me

peter-fiery-trial.text: Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you: But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy

timothy-ready-to-be-offered.text: For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand

revelation-white-robes.text: And one of the elders answered, saying unto me, What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they? And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb

quran-think-not-as-dead.text: Think not of those, who are slain in the way of Allah, as dead. Nay, they are living. With their Lord they have provision.

quran-if-thou-stretch-out-thy-hand.text: Even if thou stretch out thy hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against thee to kill thee, lo! I fear Allah, the Lord of the Worlds.

quran-bought-from-the-believers.text: Lo! Allah hath bought from the believers their lives and their wealth because the Garden will be theirs: they shall fight in the way of Allah and shall slay and be slain. It is a promise which is binding on Him in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an. Who fulfilleth His covenant better than Allah? Rejoice then in your bargain that ye have made, for that is the supreme triumph.

quran-owners-of-the-ditch.text: (Self-)destroyed were the owners of the ditch Of the fuel-fed fire, When they sat by it, And were themselves the witnesses of what they did to the believers. They had naught against them save that they believed in Allah, the Mighty, the Owner of Praise

ignatius-wheat-of-god.text: I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ
ignatius-wheat-of-god.author: Ignatius of Antioch

milton-avenge-o-lord.text: Avenge O Lord thy slaughter'd Saints, whose bones / Lie scatter'd on the Alpine mountains cold, / Ev'n them who kept thy truth so pure of old / When all our Fathers worship't Stocks and Stones
milton-avenge-o-lord.author: John Milton
milton-avenge-o-lord.work: Sonnet 18 (On the Late Massacre in Piedmont)

dickens-far-far-better-thing.text: It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done; it is a far, far better rest that I go to than I have ever known
dickens-far-far-better-thing.author: Charles Dickens

thucydides-whole-earth-for-their-tomb.text: For heroes have the whole earth for their tomb
thucydides-whole-earth-for-their-tomb.author: Thucydides
thucydides-whole-earth-for-their-tomb.locator: Book II, the funeral oration of Pericles

nietzsche-blood-worst-witness.text: Characters of blood did they write on the way they went, and their folly taught that truth is proved by blood. But blood is the very worst witness to truth
nietzsche-blood-worst-witness.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
